notes.b: Migration has its own vocabulary, and examiners expect you to use it precisely. These terms let you describe who moves, where, and why.
points: Migration is a permanent or long-term change of residence, so a holiday or a short work trip does not count.

Emigration is leaving a country; immigration is arriving in one. Net migration is immigrants minus emigrants, so it is positive when more people arrive than leave and negative when more leave than arrive.
Internal migration moves people within a country; international migration crosses borders, so it is the kind that meets immigration laws.

Voluntary migration is a free choice; forced migration is driven by conflict or persecution (being treated badly or harmed because of who you are or what you believe), so people have little or no choice.
Economic migrants move for work; refugees and asylum seekers (people who ask another country for protection) flee persecution. Asylum policy is in Migration policy in Ireland and the EU.
Return migration is emigrants coming back to their home country, such as Irish emigrants returning in the 1970s.
Chain migration is when migrants follow family or friends who have already moved, because those contacts offer information, a place to stay and help finding work.
notes.tip: You may be asked to define net migration: say it is immigrants minus emigrants.

notes.b: People move because something drives them away from home (a push factor) or something attracts them to another place (a pull factor). Ireland has examples of both.
points: Push factors in Ireland: unemployment, low wages, emigration of young people in recession (a period when the economy shrinks and jobs are lost) and the decline of farm labouring (paid work on other people's farms), which left rural workers without jobs.

Pull factors in Ireland: jobs in the Celtic Tiger economy (the period of rapid growth from the mid-1990s), high wages in the UK, the USA and Australia, and the availability of work permits (official permission to take a job in a country).
notes.tip: Exams ask for one push and one pull factor associated with migration in Ireland. Give one from each list above.

notes.b: Even when push and pull factors favour a move, obstacles can stop or reduce it. These barriers are also called intervening obstacles.
points: Distance and the cost of travel, because a longer journey costs more money and time.
Immigration laws, visas (permits to enter or stay) and quotas (limits on how many people may enter).
Language, because it is hard to work or settle where you cannot communicate.
Family ties and age: people with family at home, or older people, are less willing or able to move.
Lack of information, because people will not move to a place they know little about.
Cultural difference, such as unfamiliar customs, which makes settling in harder.
notes.tip: Exams ask for two barriers to migration. Pick two from this list and say why each stops people moving.

notes.b: Geographers have turned patterns in migration into simple models. Each gives a short rule you can use to explain why and how people move.
points: Ravenstein's laws of migration say that most migrants move short distances, in steps (for example from a village to a town and then to a city).
Ravenstein also said that each migration stream has a counter-stream (people moving the opposite way), that young adults are most likely to migrate, and that cities attract migrants.
Lee's push-pull model says migration is driven by push and pull factors and reduced by intervening obstacles (the barriers to migration listed above).

notes.b: Migrants are not a random sample of the population. Certain groups move far more than others, which shapes both the place they leave and the place they reach.
points: Migration is age-selective: mostly young adults move, because they are free to take jobs and have fewest ties.
In the 1950s more women than men left some rural areas.

notes.h: Background: emigration from the Famine to 1961
notes.b: Emigration has shaped Irish population for well over a century. The Great Famine (a disaster in the 1840s when the potato crop failed and many starved) began a long decline in numbers.
points: The Great Famine (1845-49) and continuous emigration from the 1840s: about 1 million died and about 1 million emigrated across the whole island.
The State's population fell at almost every census (the official count of the population, taken regularly) from 1841 to 1961.
State population was about 6.5 million (Census 1841), about 3.0 million (Census 1926) and about 2.8 million (Census 1961), the lowest ever recorded.
The only break in the decline was a very slight rise between Census 1946 and Census 1951.
Over 30 million Americans report Irish ancestry (US Census Bureau surveys, 2020s), a sign of how many people left.
notes.tip: The lowest census population is 1961, not 1991. The 1980s did not make the State's population fall below its 1961 level.

notes.b: The 1950s saw the highest emigration since the 1880s. Ireland was a donor region (a place people leave), and most emigrants went to Britain.
points: Causes at home: economic stagnation (no growth) and protectionism (taxing imports to shield home industry), unemployment, and the decline of small farms and farm labouring as farming mechanised and needed fewer workers.
Britain pulled workers because its post-war economy needed labour in building, factories, nursing and transport.
Low fares and the Common Travel Area made the move easy. The Common Travel Area dates from the 1920s and lets Irish citizens live and work in the UK without permits.
Chain migration also helped, as people followed relatives who had already gone.
Net emigration (people leaving minus people arriving) was about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961.
Most went to Britain: London, Birmingham, Manchester, Coventry and Liverpool.
The Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems reported in 1954.
Impact: Ireland, as donor region, lost young workers and its rural population declined.
notes.tip: The 1950s outflow was mainly to Britain, not America.

notes.b: Government policy changed direction around 1958, turning towards economic growth and foreign investment. As jobs appeared, emigration fell and, for the first time since the Famine, more people arrived than left.
points: Economic Development by T. K. Whitaker and the First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958, cut emigration.
The IDA (Industrial Development Authority), set up in 1949, was given a central role in attracting foreign investment from 1969.
The 1970s were the first decade of net immigration since the Famine: returning emigrants and their children came back, and jobs were available in new factories.
Ireland joined the EEC (the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU) on 1 January 1973.
State population rose from about 3.0 million (Census 1971) to about 3.4 million (Census 1981).
notes.tip: Don't say the 1970s had net emigration: they were net immigration.

notes.h: 1980s: emigration to Britain and the USA
notes.b: The gains of the 1970s did not last. A weak economy in the 1980s sent many people abroad again.
points: Causes: recession, high unemployment and high taxes.
Net emigration of over 200,000 between 1981 and 1991, including many graduates. This loss of educated people is the so-called brain drain.
Destinations: Britain and the USA, where many emigrants were undocumented (living and working without legal permission).
US visa programmes in the late 1980s and early 1990s (the Donnelly and Morrison visas) regularised many Irish emigrants, meaning they gained legal status.
The State's population fell slightly between Census 1986 and Census 1991; both were about 3.5 million.
notes.tip: The 1980s went to both Britain and the USA, unlike the 1950s outflow, which was mainly to Britain.

notes.b: From the mid-1990s a booming economy, nicknamed the Celtic Tiger, reversed the old pattern. Ireland now attracted workers from many countries.
points: Net immigration from 1996, as returning Irish, EU migrants, non-EU workers on work permits and asylum seekers (people seeking protection from persecution) arrived.
EU enlargement on 1 May 2004 added 10 new members, including Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovakia and the Czech Republic.
Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to open their labour markets immediately, so citizens of the new members could work here without delay.
Census 2006: about 420,000 non-Irish nationals (about 10% of the population); Polish about 63,000, the largest group after UK nationals.
Census 2006 State population was about 4.2 million.
Ireland became a country of immigration, meaning it now received more people than it sent abroad.
notes.tip: Don't say all 2004 accession states' citizens were Polish; Polish was the largest group.

notes.b: The Celtic Tiger ended abruptly in 2008, and emigration returned. Many of those leaving were the young and skilled.
points: Causes: the property crash, the banking crisis, which began in 2008, unemployment, and the EU-IMF bailout (emergency loans from the EU and International Monetary Fund) agreed in November 2010.
Net emigration from about 2009 to the mid-2010s; many leavers were skilled young graduates, and many recent immigrants also left.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013 (CSO estimate), the highest since the 1980s; about half were Irish nationals.
Main destinations: Australia, the UK, Canada and the USA. Australia's working holiday visa (a visa letting young people live and work there for a limited time) was widely used.
notes.tip: Post-2008 emigration went mainly to Australia, Canada and the UK.

notes.b: As the economy recovered, the flow reversed once more. Net immigration returned in the mid-2010s and continued.
points: Causes: economic recovery, job growth in multinationals and services, returning Irish emigrants, and non-EU skilled workers.
Ukrainians came under EU temporary protection after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022; over 100,000 people from Ukraine came to Ireland by 2024.
International protection applicants (people applying for asylum) also arrived.
Housing pressure, because more people needing homes added to demand for housing.
notes.tip: Ukrainians are under EU temporary protection, not the international protection (asylum) process.

notes.b: Population change has two parts: natural increase (births minus deaths) and net migration. Comparing them shows which one drove growth.
points: Net migration of about 190,000 between 2016 and 2022 was larger than natural increase (about 170,000), so migration was the bigger source of population growth.

notes.b: Decades of immigration have made Ireland's population much more varied. The 2022 census gives the size of the immigrant population and its main nationalities.
points: About 630,000 non-Irish nationals (about 12% of the population), plus about 170,000 dual Irish citizens (people who hold Irish and another citizenship).
Just over 1 million people (about one in five) were born outside Ireland.
Largest non-Irish groups: Polish about 94,000; UK about 83,000; Indian about 45,000; Romanian about 43,000; Lithuanian about 31,000; Brazilian about 27,000.
Polish is the most common language other than English and Irish spoken at home (Census 2016 and 2022).

notes.b: Centuries of emigration have left Irish people spread around the world. This scattered population is called the diaspora.
points: Irish communities and people of Irish descent live in Britain, the USA and Australia.

notes.h: Ireland as donor region: negative impacts
notes.b: A donor region is a place that loses people through emigration. Losing so many people, mostly young, damaged Irish communities.
points: Loss of young workers and skills (brain drain), and of the State's investment in their education, because the country paid to train people who then worked abroad.
Ageing rural population and an imbalanced age structure, because the young left and the old stayed.
Rural decline: closed schools, fewer marriages and depopulated parishes.
Lower birth rates, because fewer young adults remained to have children, and family separation.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the positive and the negative impacts of migration on Ireland. Give each impact with its reason.

notes.h: Ireland as donor region: positive impacts
notes.b: Emigration was not all loss. It also brought some benefits to Ireland.
points: Emigrant remittances (money sent home by emigrants to their families).
Less pressure on jobs and welfare, because fewer people were looking for work or needing support.
Emigrants returned with skills, capital (money to invest) and experience in the 1970s and 1990s.
Diaspora links support trade, tourism and investment.

notes.h: Ireland as receiver region: positive impacts
notes.b: A receiver region is a place that gains people through immigration. Immigration since the 1990s has brought Ireland a range of benefits.
points: Fills labour shortages in construction, health care, hospitality and technology.
Young workers pay taxes and offset ageing, because they balance a population with many older people.
New skills and enterprise (business start-ups), because migrants bring training and ideas from abroad.
Cultural diversity, such as food, sport, languages and religions.
Keeps rural schools and parishes open, because newcomers add children and residents.
Boosts population growth, as net migration was the larger component of growth in 2016-2022.

notes.h: Ireland as receiver region: negative or challenging impacts
notes.b: Rapid immigration also creates problems. Services and communities have to adjust to more people.
points: Pressure on housing, schools and health services, because more people share the same supply.
Exploitation of some migrant workers, such as being badly treated or underpaid.
Language barriers in schools, where children may not speak English or Irish.
Integration challenges (helping newcomers to take part fully in society) and racism, detailed in Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
Remittances leave Ireland, because migrants send money to families abroad.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the positive and the negative impacts of migration on Ireland. Give each impact with its reason.

notes.b: Data questions ask why immigration to Ireland increased once the recession ended. These reasons explain the rise.
points: Economic recovery and job creation, which drew workers.
Multinational investment, as large foreign-owned companies created jobs.
EU free movement, which lets citizens of EU countries live and work in Ireland.
Return of Irish emigrants.
Ireland is English-speaking and in the EU.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one reason for a trend, such as immigration rising since 2010. Give one reason from this list.

notes.b: Immigration dropped sharply in these years because the Celtic Tiger economy collapsed. Data questions ask for a reason.
points: The recession, the collapse of construction and rising unemployment, which removed the jobs that had attracted migrants.
Many EU accession migrants (those from the countries that joined in 2004) returned home.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one reason for a trend, such as immigration falling 2007-2010. Give one reason from this list.

keyTerms.definition: A permanent or long-term change of residence.
A condition in the origin area, such as unemployment or low wages, that drives people to leave.
A condition in the destination area, such as jobs or higher wages, that attracts migrants.
A barrier, such as distance, cost, visas or language, that makes migration harder.
Migration in which people follow family or friends who have already moved.
Migrants moving back to their country of origin.
The emigration of skilled and educated young people.
The arrangement dating from the 1920s that lets Irish and British citizens live and work in each other's country without permits.
Money sent home by emigrants to family in their country of origin.
EU status giving displaced people, such as Ukrainians from 2022, residence and rights without the asylum process.
People living outside their country of origin, and their descendants.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the changing patterns of migration to and from Ireland since 1950.
questions.model: In the 1950s emigration was highest since the 1880s, with about 400,000 net emigrants between 1951 and 1961, mostly to Britain, because of stagnation, unemployment, the mechanisation of farming and British demand for labour; the Commission on Emigration reported in 1954. The 1970s brought the first net immigration since the Famine, as the First Programme for Economic Expansion and foreign investment created jobs, returning emigrants arrived, and Ireland joined the EEC in 1973. The 1980s brought heavy net emigration again, of over 200,000 between 1981 and 1991, to Britain and the USA, because of recession, high unemployment and high taxes, including many graduates. The Celtic Tiger, from 1996, brought net immigration, including EU migrants after the 2004 enlargement, workers on work permits and asylum seekers; Census 2006 recorded about 420,000 non-Irish nationals. After 2008, the property crash, banking crisis and EU–IMF bailout drove net emigration to Australia, Canada, the UK and the USA, peaking at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013. From the mid-2010s, economic recovery brought net immigration again, with Ukrainians under EU temporary protection from 2022. Net migration of about 190,000 between 2016 and 2022 was larger than natural increase of about 170,000.

questions.prompt: Population movements have an impact on donor and receiver regions. Discuss with reference to Ireland.
questions.model: As a donor region in the 1950s and 1980s, Ireland lost young workers, skills and the State's investment in their education; its rural population aged and rural schools and parishes closed. Emigrants sent remittances home, reduced pressure on jobs and welfare, and some returned with skills and capital, as in the 1970s and 1990s, while diaspora links support trade, tourism and investment. As a receiver region since 1996, Ireland gained workers to fill shortages in construction, health care, hospitality and technology; young workers paid taxes and offset ageing; new skills and enterprise arrived; and cultural diversity grew. Migration also kept rural schools and parishes open and boosted population growth. The negative effects of immigration include pressure on housing, schools and health services, exploitation of some migrant workers, language barriers in schools, integration challenges and racism, and money sent abroad as remittances.

questions.prompt: Name one push factor and one pull factor associated with migration in Ireland.
questions.model: Push factor: unemployment in recession, such as the 1980s. Pull factor: jobs in the Celtic Tiger economy, from 1996.

questions.prompt: Discuss the positive impacts of migration on Ireland.
questions.model: Immigration fills labour shortages in construction, health care, hospitality and technology. Young immigrant workers pay taxes and offset the effects of an ageing population. Immigrants bring new skills and enterprise. Cultural diversity grows through food, sport, languages and religions. Migration keeps rural schools and parishes open and boosts population growth, with net migration the larger component of growth from 2016 to 2022. Emigrants returning from abroad bring skills, capital and experience, as in the 1970s and 1990s.
